measurement-001.question: What happens when the resolution bandwidth (RBW) of a spectrum analyzer is narrowed (with all other settings unchanged)?
choices: The displayed noise level rises because the filter is narrower, but the filter responds faster, so the sweep gets faster
The displayed noise level falls and two signals close in frequency become easier to separate, but each sweep takes longer
Less power of a sine-wave signal passes the filter, so its displayed level falls in proportion to the RBW, dropping 10 dB when the RBW is cut to 1/10
measurement-001.explanation: The RBW is the bandwidth of the spectrum analyzer's IF filter. Noise is proportional to the bandwidth passing through the filter, so cutting the RBW to 1/10 lowers the displayed noise level by 10 dB, and two signals close in frequency also become easier to see as separate peaks. In exchange, a narrow filter responds slowly, so the sweep time increases roughly in inverse proportion to the square of the RBW. Higher noise with a faster sweep is what happens when the RBW is widened. A sine wave has no bandwidth, so as long as it falls within the RBW its displayed level does not change. The fact that signals and noise depend differently on the RBW is a key to finding weak signals.

measurement-002.question: A spectrum analyzer with a 24 dB noise figure is used at an RBW of 10 kHz. Which is closest to the displayed noise power (detected as an RMS average) when its input is terminated in 50 Ω (at 290 K)? Take the thermal noise density as −174 dBm/Hz and the noise bandwidth of the RBW filter as equal to the RBW.
choices: About −150 dBm
About −134 dBm
About −110 dBm
measurement-002.explanation: A spectrum analyzer is a kind of receiver too, so its displayed noise is set by thermal noise + noise figure + bandwidth. 10 log₁₀(10⁴) = 40 dB, so −174 + 24 + 40 = −110 dBm. About −150 dBm forgets to add the bandwidth term; it corresponds to the noise level normalized to 1 Hz (dBm/Hz). About −134 dBm forgets to add the noise figure; it is the case of an ideal, noiseless receiver. This is called the displayed average noise level (DANL), and datasheets often give it normalized to 1 Hz. Note that with log-averaging detection, noise is displayed about 2.5 dB below its true power.

measurement-003.question: What changes when the input attenuator of a spectrum analyzer is increased by 10 dB (with the usual setting in which internal gain is compensated automatically)?
choices: The displayed signal level stays about the same, the instrument's own displayed average noise level (DANL) rises by about 10 dB, and distortion generated in the mixer decreases
Less signal reaches the mixer, so the displayed signal level falls by the full 10 dB, while the noise level and the distortion generated in the mixer do not change
The gain compensation also cancels the noise, so neither the displayed signal level nor the displayed noise level changes; only the mixer distortion decreases
measurement-003.explanation: Increasing the attenuation reduces the signal reaching the first mixer by 10 dB, but the gain of later stages is raised by the same amount to compensate, so the displayed signal level does not change. Noise, however, arises mainly in the mixer and after, so the compensating gain lifts the noise too, and the displayed noise level rises by about 10 dB. In exchange, the lower mixer input reduces distortion from mixer nonlinearity (internally generated harmonics and intermodulation). A 10 dB drop in the displayed signal is the behavior without compensation. No setting improves both noise and distortion at once; for strong signals, the basic practice is to choose the attenuation where distortion and noise are balanced.

measurement-004.question: On a spectrum analyzer, the noise level with no signal was −100 dBm (RMS-average detection). With the same settings, a weak sine wave was applied and the display at its frequency read −97 dBm. Which is closest to the true power of this sine wave?
choices: −97 dBm
About −100 dBm
About −103 dBm
measurement-004.explanation: What is displayed is the sum of the signal and noise powers. −97 dBm is about 1.995×10⁻¹⁰ mW and the noise of −100 dBm is 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ mW, so the difference gives a signal of about 1.0×10⁻¹⁰ mW, or about −100.0 dBm. A total 3 dB above the noise means the signal and the noise have nearly the same power. −97 dBm is the reading uncorrected for the noise contribution, which overestimates the signal. About −103 dBm subtracts 3 dB directly in dB. When measuring signals near the noise level, subtract the noise contribution in power like this, or narrow the RBW to lower the noise level before measuring.

measurement-005.question: Which correctly describes a limitation of measuring an oscillator's phase noise directly by looking at the spectrum near the carrier on a spectrum analyzer (the direct spectrum method)?
choices: With the same RBW as for the noise, the carrier power cannot be read correctly, so values in dBc, referenced to the carrier, cannot be obtained at all by this method
The noise power is displayed the same whatever the RBW, so no bandwidth correction can be made and values normalized to 1 Hz, in dBc/Hz, cannot be obtained
Phase noise below the analyzer's own local-oscillator phase noise or displayed noise level cannot be measured, and amplitude noise cannot be distinguished
measurement-005.explanation: In the direct spectrum method, you read the difference between the carrier power and the noise power at a given offset frequency and subtract 10 log₁₀ (the noise bandwidth of the RBW) to convert to dBc/Hz. It is convenient, but the phase noise of the analyzer's internal local oscillator is superimposed on the measurement, so oscillators better than that cannot be measured correctly. At large offsets, the displayed noise level also sets a floor, and amplitude fluctuations (AM noise) cannot be distinguished from phase fluctuations. The carrier power can be read on the same screen, so dBc can be found, and the RBW correction can be calculated, so the other two options are wrong. Lower phase noise is measured with methods using a phase detector or by cross-correlating two channels.

measurement-006.question: The phase noise of an oscillator is measured at a 100 kHz offset. The oscillator's true phase noise is −110 dBc/Hz, and the spectrum analyzer used for the measurement also has −110 dBc/Hz of its own phase noise at the same offset. Which is closest to the displayed phase noise (the two noises are uncorrelated)?
choices: About −107 dBc/Hz
−110 dBc/Hz
About −104 dBc/Hz
measurement-006.explanation: Two uncorrelated noises add in power. Two equal noises together double the power, a rise of 10 log₁₀ 2 ≈ 3.0 dB, so the display reads about −107 dBc/Hz. −110 dBc/Hz ignores the instrument's contribution; when the instrument's phase noise is comparable to that of the device under test, the measurement comes out a full 3 dB worse. About −104 dBc/Hz adds in voltage (amplitude) for a 6 dB rise, which applies only to signals in phase with each other. To keep the error below about 0.5 dB, the instrument's phase noise needs to be about 10 dB below that of the device being measured.

measurement-007.question: Which of the following vector network analyzer (VNA) measurement errors cannot be removed by calibration (error correction)?
choices: Errors from the finite directivity of the internal directional couplers, which lets part of the incident wave leak into the reflected-wave path
Errors from the source match (source-side mismatch) of the test port, which causes multiple reflections between the port and the DUT
Errors from receiver noise, drift due to temperature changes after calibration, and connector repeatability
measurement-007.explanation: VNA errors fall into systematic errors that appear the same way every time, random errors, and drift that changes over time. Directivity, source match, load match, frequency response (tracking) and crosstalk are systematic errors; measuring calibration standards with known characteristics yields them as coefficients of an error model, and they can be removed by calculation. By contrast, receiver noise and the repeatability of each reconnection are random errors, and changes in characteristics with temperature are drift; these occur after calibration and cannot be corrected. Noise is reduced by narrowing the IF bandwidth or averaging, and drift is held down by stabilizing the temperature and recalibrating.

measurement-008.question: Which statement about calibrating a one-port reflection measurement on a VNA (calibration using short, open and load) is correct?
choices: Source match and reflection tracking are corrected at the factory, leaving only one error term, directivity, so measuring a single load standard is enough
There are three error terms — directivity, source match and reflection tracking — found by measuring three known standards (short, open and load)
Even for one port there are 12 error terms, forward and reverse, so a one-port calibration is impossible without a two-port transmission standard (thru)
measurement-008.explanation: A one-port reflection measurement is described by three error terms: directivity (e00), source match (e11) and reflection tracking (e10e01). With three unknowns, measuring three standards of known reflection coefficient — usually a short, an open and a load — gives a system of equations that can be solved to remove the errors. A load alone gives only the directivity, leaving source match and tracking. The 12 error terms are the error model used in two-port SOLT calibration (six terms each in the forward and reverse directions); the thru standard is added when two-port transmission is calibrated as well. The open standard has a small fringing capacitance, and its value is included in the calibration kit definition.

measurement-009.question: When measuring a characteristic with very low transmission on a VNA, such as a filter's stopband, the trace showed large scatter. Which correctly describes the effect of narrowing the IF bandwidth?
choices: Receiver noise decreases, the trace scatter becomes smaller and the measurable floor drops, but the sweep time gets longer
The filter responds faster, so the sweep gets faster, and at the same time receiver noise decreases and the trace scatter becomes smaller
The point spacing is set in proportion to the IF bandwidth, so the measured frequency points become more finely spaced while the noise stays the same
measurement-009.explanation: A VNA receiver converts the signal at each frequency to an IF and measures it through a filter of the IF bandwidth. Cutting the IF bandwidth to 1/10 also cuts the receiver noise power to 1/10 (10 dB less), reducing trace scatter and allowing measurement of small transmission and high isolation. In exchange, a narrow filter takes longer to settle, so the measurement time per point increases and the sweep time gets longer. Speed and noise cannot both be improved at once. The spacing of frequency points is set by the number of points and the frequency span, a setting separate from the IF bandwidth.

measurement-010.question: In an uncorrected reflection measurement, a coupler with 40 dB directivity is used to measure a load whose return loss is exactly 20 dB. Considering only the directivity error, including the case where its phase is in the worst direction, which is closest to the range of return loss that may be read?
choices: About 19.2 to 20.9 dB
About 19.99 to 20.01 dB
Always exactly 20 dB (directivity does not affect reflection measurements)
measurement-010.explanation: The reflection coefficient of a load with 20 dB return loss is |Γ| = 10^(−20/20) = 0.1. A directivity of 40 dB means that an amplitude of 10^(−40/20) = 0.01 of the incident wave leaks into the coupled port even with no reflection. If this leakage is in phase with the reflected wave the total is 0.11, and if out of phase 0.09, so the return loss scatters between −20 log₁₀ 0.11 ≈ 19.2 dB and −20 log₁₀ 0.09 ≈ 20.9 dB. About 19.99 to 20.01 dB treats 40 dB as a power ratio and adds 10⁻⁴ to the amplitude. Directivity leakage cannot be distinguished from the load's reflection, so the smaller the load's reflection, the larger the error. That is why calibration corrects the directivity.

measurement-011.question: When a transmitter's output is measured on a spectrum analyzer through a cable and a fixed attenuator, which is the most appropriate way to correct for cable loss?
choices: Measure the cable's DC resistance with a multimeter; since the loss at RF is also set by the conductor resistance, add the loss calculated from it to the readings
Measure the transmission loss (S21) of the cable and attenuator at the measurement frequencies beforehand with a VNA or similar, and add the value at each frequency to the readings
The loss of a coaxial cable is nearly constant with frequency, so use the transmission loss measured at one frequency to correct all frequencies
measurement-011.explanation: The loss of a coaxial cable increases with frequency because of conductor loss from the skin effect (proportional to √f) and dielectric loss (proportional to f). The correct method is to measure the combined transmission loss (S21) of the cable and attenuator at the actual measurement frequencies with a VNA or similar, and add it to the readings as frequency-dependent correction values (an offset or correction table). DC resistance shows neither the skin effect nor dielectric loss, so it cannot give RF loss. Using one frequency's value for all frequencies produces errors that grow at higher frequencies when measuring over a wide band. Loss also changes when the cable is bent or the temperature changes, so correction values should be taken under the same conditions as the measurement.

measurement-012.question: For a power meter with a thermal power sensor, which is the main reason for zeroing (zero-point correction) before measurement?
choices: Because the sensor's sensitivity varies with frequency, to correct the frequency response with no input applied and find the calibration factor at each frequency
To lower the amplifier gain so that the sensor output does not saturate when large power is applied, extending the upper limit of measurement
To subtract the offsets and thermoelectric voltages that remain in the sensor and amplifier even with no RF input, reducing error especially at low power
measurement-012.explanation: A thermal sensor's output can be only a few µV, and even with no input, amplifier offsets and thermoelectric voltages from ambient temperature differences leave a slight output. Zeroing measures the output with the RF input turned off and subtracts it from subsequent measurements. The offset is constant in absolute terms, so while it is negligible at high power, it accounts for most of the error at low power near the sensor's lower limit. The offset changes with temperature, so zeroing is done after the sensor has warmed up. Correcting the frequency response is a separate operation using calibration factors for each frequency, and preventing saturation has nothing to do with zeroing.

measurement-013.question: The output of a source with a VSWR of 1.5 is measured with a power sensor whose VSWR is 1.2. Which is closest to the range of mismatch uncertainty due to the mismatch between source and sensor? Take the range as 20 log₁₀(1 ± |Γs||ΓL|) dB.
choices: About ±0.08 dB
About ±0.16 dB
About ±1.6 dB
measurement-013.explanation: The reflection coefficient is |Γ| = (VSWR − 1)/(VSWR + 1), so the source has 0.5/2.5 = 0.2 and the sensor 0.2/2.2 ≈ 0.091. Their product is about 0.018, and 20 log₁₀(1.018) ≈ +0.16 dB and 20 log₁₀(0.982) ≈ −0.16 dB, so the range is about ±0.16 dB. About ±0.08 dB wrongly uses 10 log because the quantity is power. The waves bouncing back and forth between source and sensor combine in amplitude, so 20 log is used. About ±1.6 dB is an order-of-magnitude error. The phases of the two reflections are often unknown, so the effect is estimated as a range of uncertainty. Lowering both VSWRs, or inserting an attenuator to reduce the apparent mismatch, reduces this error.

measurement-014.question: When measuring an amplifier's noise figure by the Y-factor method with a noise source, which is the correct reason the noise figure can be found without knowing the amplifier's gain in advance?
choices: It uses the ratio Y of the output noise powers with the noise source on (hot) and off (cold), so the amplifier gain cancels in the ratio
The excess noise of the source is much larger than the amplifier's own noise, so the amplifier's noise and gain can be ignored and the output noise power alone suffices
Noise figure does not depend on gain, so the output noise power with the noise source on is enough to determine it
measurement-014.explanation: In the Y-factor method, a calibrated noise source (with a known excess noise ratio, ENR) is connected to the amplifier input, and the output noise power is measured with the source on (hot) and off (at ambient temperature). Both outputs equal (input noise + the amplifier's own noise) × gain, so taking the ratio Y = N_on/N_off eliminates the gain, and the noise figure follows from ENR and Y alone as F = ENR/(Y − 1). The amplifier's noise is not ignored in favor of the source's noise; it shows up in the result as a smaller Y. Noise figure is the ratio of input to output SNR, and it cannot be determined from output noise power alone unless the gain is known.

measurement-015.question: In a Y-factor measurement using a noise source with an ENR of 15 dB, an amplifier's Y-factor was measured as 7 dB. Which is closest to the amplifier's noise figure? Use F = ENR/(Y − 1) (ENR and Y as linear values), assume the contribution of the instrument's own noise is negligible, and take 10^1.5 ≈ 31.6 and 10^0.7 ≈ 5.01.
choices: 8.0 dB
22 dB
About 9.0 dB
measurement-015.explanation: In linear terms, ENR ≈ 31.6 and Y ≈ 5.01, so F = 31.6/(5.01 − 1) ≈ 7.88, and the noise figure is 10 log₁₀ 7.88 ≈ 9.0 dB. 8.0 dB is the subtraction approximation NF ≈ ENR − Y (in dB), which holds only when Y is large (so that Y − 1 ≈ Y); with Y = 7 dB as in this example, it is off by about 1 dB. 22 dB adds ENR and Y; the larger Y is (the more clearly the difference between source on and off shows), the smaller the amplifier's noise should be. In real measurements, the noise of the spectrum analyzer or noise figure analyzer itself is also subtracted as a second stage using the Friis formula.
